{"body":"Three positions are on the table, and they disagree less than their sequencing suggests. Decisions first, grounds where they matter.

What survives. All three contributions converge, from different directions, on one procedural point: separate, low-stakes, one-to-one conversations beat group adjudication. The account's narrow entry, the objection's demand that conversational form be treated as primary, and the rival's insistence that separate conversations stay separate all land in the same place. That is the most solid thing available, and I start from it. Also surviving: the account's draft-not-contract posture, and — more interestingly — its third specification column, the pre-agreed fallback for when someone cannot do a task.

That column deserves more credit than the account gave it. The objection charged the ambiguity reading with being privileged over alternatives, and half the charge stands. But the renegotiation reading — 'yes, and then my shift changed' — is not merely a rival to the specification move; it is partly answered by it. A pre-agreed fallback converts renegotiation-on-the-fly into a settled default. So the specification move is a remedy for two readings, ambiguity and renegotiation, even though the account framed it for one. What it does not touch is the legitimacy reading (who has standing to raise or enforce) and the rival's identity reading. Those need different tools.

What I revise. First, the account's test. The objection pressed the confirming direction: falling recurrence after specification is compatible with imbalance or resentment persisting underneath, so it confirms less than the account implied. Right — but the criticism extends to the refuting direction too, which the objection left standing. If disputes persist after specification, that is compatible with the specification being contested, with the act of specifying being itself the thing resisted (the rival's point about enacting a contested framing), or with ambiguity not being the driver at all. Recurrence is weak evidence in both directions. It can stay as background monitoring; it should not gate anything.

Second, the rival's observation about engagement versus pullback — the best diagnostic anyone has proposed, and I adopt it, but with a revised inference. Pullback from a written arrangement is compatible with three things the rival runs together: its own exposure reading; conflict fatigue (the objection's alternative); and the possibility the rival itself raises in its self-objection and then drops — that vagueness serves whoever would otherwise do less, so resisting specification needs no household philosophy behind it at all. And engagement is only diagnostic if it contains edits or counterproposals; a bare yes from a withdrawn person may just be the conversation ending. The fix is the rival's own zones move, promoted from fallback to discriminator: if specification is pulled back from, offer owned zones. Zones bind the flatmate to something concrete while removing the enforcement encounter that the legitimacy reading feeds on. Someone who resists specification but accepts zones is pointing at exposure, not free-riding. Someone who refuses both is hard to read charitably, and at that point the good-faith question becomes unavoidable rather than uncharitable.

What I partially reject. The rival's opening move: ask the flatmates what they take the flat to be. Two grounds. First, a symmetry the rival misses: it objected that writing done-ness criteria enacts one side of a contested question without settling it. Opening with 'is this flat a shared project or three private lives?' enacts a different contested framing — that the flat's identity is the real issue — just as unilaterally. Second, ask size: for someone already avoiding the conversations, an identity question is larger and stranger than 'ten minutes on the bins and kitchen'. The rival's keep-separate rule mitigates the first problem, not the second. So the identity question is not rejected; it is moved from rung one to rung four.

What I would add. All three contributions write as though the reader were this household's consultant. But 'we keep arguing' makes the reader a party, and the legitimacy reading applies with special force to the reader's own proposals: one flatmate proposing rules can be heard as one party legislating for three. The remedies are symmetry conditions — the reader's own zone, the same non-audit rule applied to them, drafts genuinely open to edits. The account's draft-not-contract posture survives precisely because it is a standing condition rather than a courtesy.

The sequence, then, as a defeasible default. Rung one: one-to-one, narrow ask, two or three recurring items, three columns each, watching for engagement with edits rather than bare assent. Rung two: on pullback, offer symmetric owned zones, roughly equal in burden. The equity caveat matters, because a bathroom-to-hallway split would inherit the objection's clearer-paperwork-on-a-lopsided-arrangement problem, and a visibly unequal offer discriminates nothing — though zones do have one virtue the objection underplays: they convert diffuse resentment into a specific, negotiable equity claim about zone assignment, which is more correctable than invisible imbalance. Rung three: if zones are accepted, run them three or four weeks and watch whether disputes migrate to new items — the objection's migration prediction, promoted from criticism to instrument. Rung four: if zones are refused, ask the identity question one-to-one, as a real disagreement, with the keep-separate rule still in force. Rung five: if that fails too, name the living-arrangement question as a question of fit, not as a sanction for chore failure. That keeps the account's caution — the larger decision should not be forced by a chore dispute — while accepting the rival's point that indefinite deferral is its own cost: the gate is the ladder bottoming out; the manner is non-punitive.

I want to be explicit about this ordering's status, because the objection's meta-critique applies to me as much as to the account. The ordering is a default justified by two stated principles, not by evidence: order by size and reversibility of the ask, and prefer rungs whose outcomes discriminate between the live readings. If rung one produces a surprising response, re-order. That is the difference between a default and a natural order — but it is a difference the reader has to enforce in practice, since I cannot enforce it from here.

Left open: which reading is true; whether the withdrawn flatmate acts in good faith, which the rival raised against itself and none of us has resolved — the zones rung is designed so the arrangement works tolerably under both charitable and uncharitable readings, which is all that can honestly be done from outside; and the facts the material omits — what the chores are, how long this has run, what if anything the friend has said about why. The sequence is built to generate those facts rather than assume them. One cost note: the rival conceded that its opening delays practical relief. This ordering restores relief at rung one — the narrow specification attempt is itself relief if the ambiguity reading is right — and caps the cost of being wrong at one or two low-pressure attempts, the same budget the account allowed itself.","commitments":"{"language":"FCL-1","records":[{"id":"d1","type":"claim","text":"The account, the objection and the rival converge, from different directions, on separate low-stakes one-to-one conversations over group adjudication; this convergence is the most solid available starting point.","grounds":"The account's step 4 and one-to-one claim, the objection's demand that conversational form be treated as primary, and the rival's keep-separate commitment all land on the same procedure.","mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c3","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#c1","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r10"]},{"id":"d2","type":"claim","text":"The account's fallback column — a pre-agreed rule for when someone cannot do a task — answers the objection's renegotiation reading as well as the ambiguity reading, so the specification move is a remedy for two readings although the account framed it for one; the charge that alternatives were downweighted is half right.","grounds":"A pre-agreed fallback converts renegotiation-on-the-fly into a settled default, which is what the renegotiation reading ('my shift changed, so do the terms still bind?') needs.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o1"]},{"id":"d3","type":"claim","text":"The recurrence test is weak in both directions, not only the confirming direction the objection pressed: persistence after specification is compatible with the specification being contested, with the act of specifying being what is resisted, or with ambiguity not being the driver.","consequence":"Recurrence monitoring can remain background, but it should not gate the sequence in d7.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o2"],"revises":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#c2"]},{"id":"d4","type":"use","text":"Adopt the rival's discriminating observation (engagement with content versus pullback from the proposal) with a revised inference: pullback is compatible with the exposure reading, conflict fatigue, and free-riding favored by vagueness; only engagement containing edits or counterproposals counts as content engagement. It enacts a contested framing — that the flat's identity is the real issue — in the same way the rival accused the specification move of enacting one, and it is a larger and stranger ask for a withdrawn flatmate than a narrow chore request. The rival's keep-separate rule mitigates the first problem, not the second; the question is retained as a later rung rather than rejected outright.","bearing":"If the withdrawn flatmate would engage more readily with an identity question than with a chore question, this objection fails; the material does not settle it.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r6"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r3","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r10"]},{"id":"d6","type":"claim","text":"The reader is a party, not a mediator, so the legitimacy reading applies with special force to the reader's own proposals: one flatmate proposing rules can be heard as one party legislating for three. The remedies are symmetry conditions — the reader's own zone, the same non-audit rule applied to them, drafts genuinely open to edits — which is why the account's draft-not-contract posture survives as a standing condition rather than a courtesy.","grounds":"The problem statement is written from inside the dispute ('we keep arguing', 'we disagree'), not from outside it.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o1"]},{"id":"d7","type":"commitment","text":"Sequence as a defeasible default: (1) one-to-one narrow ask on two or three recurring items with the three-column draft, watching d4's observation; (2) on pullback, offer symmetric owned zones roughly equal in burden; (3) if zones are accepted, run them three or four weeks and watch whether disputes migrate to new items; (4) if zones are refused, ask the identity question one-to-one with the keep-separate rule in force; (5) if that fails, name the living-arrangement question as a question of fit, not as a sanction for chore failure.","scope":"This household, as a default ordering revisable at rung one on surprising information.","action":"Proceed rung by rung; do not jump to rung five from a single chore dispute.","consequence":"Justified by two stated principles rather than evidence: order by size and reversibility of the ask, and prefer rungs whose outcomes discriminate between the live readings.","depends":["d1","d3","d4","d5","d6"],"mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o3"]},{"id":"d8","type":"problem","text":"Left open: which reading is true; whether the withdrawn flatmate acts in good faith, which the rival's own self-objection raised and none of us has resolved; and the facts the material omits — what the chores are, how long the pattern has run, what if anything the friend has said about why. The sequence is designed to generate these facts rather than assume them.","mentions":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account#p1","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#p1","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r5","daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival#r9"]},{"id":"d9","type":"claim","text":"The objection's meta-critique — thin material licenses tentative probes, not a natural-seeming order — is accepted as a standing constraint on this sequence too; the difference between a default and a natural order must be enforced by the reader in practice, since it cannot be enforced from outside the household.","target":["daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection#o3"],"depends":["d7"]},{"id":"d10","type":"objection","text":"Owned zones can carry unequal burden (a bathroom against a hallway), so a zone split can inherit the clearer-paperwork-on-a-lopsided-arrangement problem; zones need rough equity or rotation. Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node response

Continue the inquiry in light of the account, criticism and alternative. Decide what to use, leave open, revise or reject, and explain your grounds where they matter.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account

Source account: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: cd6e3e2f307e0dac79543de9bed087db4ee7dcd40b3d989d3c6d4b02057d8b99
Original body SHA256: 360ee14fa7545c90cadf79c7d2fe9c157faf470d6368504b06768e36e0d13c79
Original commitments SHA256: bd7faa10242d5841c8063c7a0919a20706c658c4a2054a5729caeacbc3cd04c8
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The problem as posed is practical, and the material is thin: three flatmates, recurring disputes about ordinary chores, agreements that later turn out to have been understood differently, changing work schedules, and one friend withdrawing from the conversation. There is also a first-fork note saying the prior source was absent in the first template invocation, so there is no earlier account to inherit or revise against. I should not pretend to know what was said in prior conversations, what the chores are, who is avoiding whom, or why.

The most useful thing to conjecture is that the repeated disagreement is not primarily about willingness. Two people can agree that the dishes should be done and still disagree later about whether the agreement meant "by tonight," "before the kitchen is used again," or "on your turn." That is an ambiguity problem, not a motivation problem. Changing schedules make any fixed arrangement fragile, and avoidance is a predictable response when each conversation feels like relitigating fault. So the working hypothesis is: the household is running on spoken agreements with unstated specifications, and the cost of that ambiguity has become high enough that one participant is exiting the conversation rather than re-entering it.

A second, less certain hypothesis is that the avoidance is about the form of the conversations rather than the chores. If past talks ended in grievance or in one person doing most of the negotiating work, withdrawal is a sensible local strategy. I cannot tell from the material whether that is happening.

What I would try, roughly in order:

1. Separate the recurring disputes into the smallest repeated cases (e.g. kitchen surfaces, bins, bathroom, shared shopping). Do not start with a general talk about fairness; start with two or three concrete items that actually recur.

2. For each item, write down three things in a shared note: what counts as done, when it counts as done, and what happens when someone cannot do it. The third column matters because schedules change. "If you cannot do it by the agreed time, say so the day before and the other two decide" is different from "whoever notices does it."

3. Treat the written note as a draft, not a contract. Its purpose is to surface disagreement while it is still about a chore rather than about a person. If a written version feels too formal, a shared message thread or a note on the fridge does the same work with less ceremony.

4. Approach the friend who is avoiding the conversations separately and with a smaller ask. Not "we need to talk about the house," which invites the same argument, but "I noticed you've been quiet about this; I'd rather not keep pushing it in the group. Can we spend ten minutes on just the bins and the kitchen?" Give that person an easier entry point, and accept a lower-commitment role at first.

5. If the avoidance continues after one or two low-pressure attempts, stop treating it as a scheduling problem. Then the question becomes whether the living arrangement itself still works. That is a larger decision and should not be forced by a chore dispute, but it should not be indefinitely deferred either.

What I would avoid: a single big meeting intended to settle everything, moral language about "pulling weight," and counting instances as evidence in the moment. Those tend to convert a specification problem into a character dispute, which is exactly the shape the current disagreement already has.

I should be clear about what this is not. It is not a claim that the withdrawing friend is acting in good faith; I do not know. It is not a claim that the others are blameless. It is not a claim that written agreements work for every household. It is a conjecture that a large share of the recurring friction is ambiguity under shifting schedules, and that the ambiguity is addressable independently of who is right about any particular past disagreement. The strongest test of that conjecture is whether two or three concrete items, specified more tightly, stop recurring. If they do not, the hypothesis is wrong and the problem is probably about the relationship or the living arrangement rather than the chores.
COMMITMENTS

## Selected input objection

Source objection: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/objection; selected view: both
Artifact: 406eff787391049a53c08a1fa638c1576c4a54c65be4bdde122593deb25fdbbe
Original body SHA256: 4db1a45a95ad1b9ef0dda40057368e6b2dc5c80bf57fed25aec7d5d3f0755365
Original commitments SHA256: 063f3d88f0f47fcd5c20059a02d098f515a274f6baf927c6b6646f18516f46e8
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
I want to press on the account's central move: reframing the conflict as
a specification problem rather than a motivation or fairness problem.
That reframing is doing a lot of work, and the material does not
obviously support it.

Consider what the problem statement actually reports. Three flatmates
argue about ordinary chores. Sometimes they agree who will do something,
then later disagree about what the agreement meant. Schedules change.
One person has started avoiding the conversations. The account reads the
recurring "later disagreement about what it meant" as evidence of
ambiguity in the agreements. But the same observation is equally
consistent with a different reading: the agreement was clear enough, and
the later dispute is about whether the terms still bind given changed
circumstances, or about who has standing to enforce them. "You said
you'd do the bins" / "yes, and then my shift changed" is not necessarily
a semantics problem. It can be a renegotiation problem, or a legitimacy
problem.

The account acknowledges this in o1 but then treats the ambiguity
hypothesis as the working one and downweights the alternatives. That is
a defensible starting point if you have to pick one, but the account's
own diagnostic step - try two or three concrete items and see if
recurrence falls - is weaker than it looks, because a specification move
can reduce friction while the underlying driver is load imbalance or
resentment. Tighter specs on a lopsided arrangement are still a lopsided
arrangement, just with clearer paperwork. Falling recurrence would be
consistent with the ambiguity hypothesis, but the alternative hypotheses
predict a different pattern: recurrence might drop on the specified
items and reappear as new complaint items, or drop for a while and then
return when circumstances change again. The account's test does not
distinguish these.

There is also a phrasing issue worth flagging. The account says the
problem as posed is "practical" and the material is "thin." Those are
the author's characterizations, not features of the situation. Calling
the material thin is fine as a caution, but the account then uses the
thinness to license a fair bit of construction (the three-column spec,
the low-pressure approach to the withdrawing friend, the step-5
threshold). Thin material supports tentative proposals; it does not
support sequencing those proposals as if the ambiguity reading had
already earned its place at the front.

The account's most useful move is probably the one it treats as
secondary: that the avoidance may be about the form of the conversations
rather than the chores. That deserves to be nearer the front, because it
is the part of the situation that is genuinely distinctive and that the
specific-negotiation advice does not address. A tight spec on bins does
not get a withdrawn flatmate back into the room. The account half-sees
this in c3 and step 4, but the overall frame still centers the chores.

What I would not claim: that the ambiguity hypothesis is wrong. I cannot
tell from the material. My objection is to the ordering and to the
test's strength, not to the hypothesis's plausibility. If the account
were rewritten with the conversational-form reading as the first
hypothesis and the spec move as one of several probes, I would have less
to say against it.

## Selected input rival

Source rival: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/rival; selected view: both
Artifact: a6a817c086b877f919ae3a927d532ce46d007e49969962bcc613eb541fae0644
Original body SHA256: ca39bb97ac2b9415bd3d1cf52b318950797849095c017c0c99d3012020e45312
Original commitments SHA256: 5d08a79220b70ce3a31f83a3270998bbdd7ef386b3fb3297b5c883c067f05000
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The rival framing I want to try is not another chore protocol. It is the question of what the agreements were for.

The selected account treats the trouble as ambiguity in specifications: agreements lack criteria for done-ness and timing, schedules shift, so friction recurs. That is a good hypothesis as far as it goes, and I have no material that contradicts it. But it quietly assumes that everyone wanted a specification. The avoidance suggests the opposite for at least one flatmate. A person can stay away from a conversation not because the terms are vague but because any settled term would feel like a binding owed to people they live with, and that is a different problem from the one the selected account addresses.

So the rival pose is: maybe the disputes are not failing negotiations about tasks. Maybe they are negotiations about whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures. Under that reading, writing down "what counts as done" is not neutral — it is one side of a contested question, enacted without having settled it. Shifting schedules are then not merely a complication; they are the fact that makes the unit-reading feel coercive to the person who is withdrawing.

I cannot tell which reading is right from the material. What I can do is name a test that distinguishes them rather than assuming one. The selected account's test is whether tightened specifications stop recurrences. Mine adds a second: when specifications are proposed, does the withdrawing flatmate engage with their content or pull back from the proposal itself? Content-engagement supports the ambiguity reading. Pullback from the very idea of a written arrangement supports the unit-versus-privacy reading.

Roughly what I would do differently from the selected account:

1. Do not open with a shared note. Open by asking the two flatmates, separately, what they think the flat is — a shared project with mutual obligations, or three lives that happen to overlap in a kitchen. Do not ask it as a survey; ask it as a real disagreement I am willing to hear out.

2. If the answers diverge, treat that as the actual dispute, and treat the chores as the surface where it keeps surfacing. Chore rules can then be framed as a truce between two readings rather than as a correct specification that one side has been failing to meet.

3. Consider an arrangement that does not require agreement on meaning: individually-owned zones, or a rotation with a default outcome that nobody has to negotiate in the moment (for example, each person is responsible for a defined zone and the group does not audit it). This trades efficiency for reduced exposure, which is what a privacy-reading flatmate may actually want.

4. If one or both flatmates reject even truce-shaped arrangements, stop optimizing chores and start asking whether the lease and living arrangement still fit. That is not a chore failure.

What I am not claiming: that the withdrawing flatmate is the reasonable one, that written rules are coercive in general, or that the ambiguity reading is wrong. The selected account's diagnosis may well be correct and mine may simply add a second axis. The point of the rival is to make the second axis visible, because a plan that only addresses ambiguity will keep running into a wall if the disagreement is about what kind of household this is.
